transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi. I'm here because... well, I just can't seem to shake this feeling that work isn't safe anymore. And I feel like I'm somehow damaged now. It's like the competent person who got promoted just... isn't really there anymore.
Did something specific happen at work or elsewhere that caused you to start feeling this way, or did these feelings develop gradually over time?

Yeah, it was a specific event. Um, this has all been going on since a break-in at the office. It happened during an overnight deployment I was working on... that was about two years and four months ago.
Since the break-in happened over two years ago, have these feelings about work not being safe and feeling damaged been present continuously the whole time, or have they come and gone?

Um, I'm not entirely sure, to be honest. I haven't really kept track of whether it comes and goes, or if it's just been there every single day. I just know it's... it's been an ongoing issue since it happened, and I haven't really been able to get back to how I was before.
Do you find yourself having unwanted memories, flashbacks, or nightmares about the break-in that come back to you involuntarily?

Yeah, I do. It's usually triggered by specific things... like if I hear a badge scanner beeping, or heavy footsteps out in the hallway. Even just getting a late-night deployment alert can do it. It just... it suddenly puts me right back in that office. My chest gets really tight, and the image of the guard on the floor just cuts right through whatever I’m doing at the time. So, yeah, they definitely come back involuntarily.
Since the break-in, have you been avoiding certain places, people, or situations at work because they remind you of what happened, or because you're worried something similar might happen again?

Yeah, I have. Um... I've actually started trading my shifts so I don't have to work nights. And I push back on the release windows, too, just to avoid being there late. If I do have to go in, I take the side entrance, or I just try to work from home whenever I can. Walking through that main lobby after dark... it just makes me feel like I'm going to come apart. So I just try to avoid it however I can.

You mentioned feeling damaged and that the competent person you were isn't really there anymore. Since the break-in, have your beliefs about yourself as a person changed — like do you blame yourself for what happened, or do you see yourself differently in some fundamental way?

Yeah, I do. I just... I keep thinking that if I had insisted on better security for the overnight deployment, or if I had called for help sooner, the guard might not have been hurt so badly. I mean, part of me knows I was hiding and I was just completely terrified, but I still blame myself. It makes me feel like I failed, and I definitely see myself differently because of it.
Beyond the anxiety and fear related to the break-in, have you noticed changes in your mood — like feeling persistently sad, empty, irritable, or numb to things that used to bring you pleasure?

No, I don't think so. Um... I mean, the anxiety is definitely there, like I said, but I wouldn't say I feel sad or empty all the time. And I still enjoy doing things outside of work, like my hobbies or hanging out with friends, as long as it's away from the office. So I haven't really felt numb or lost interest in stuff. It's really just the fear and the guilt that I'm dealing with right now.
Since the break-in, have you noticed that you're more jumpy or easily startled by sudden noises or movements, even when you know logically that there's no real danger?

Yeah, I definitely have. It's like I'm always on guard now. Um, on the train, in meetings, even just at lunch with my team... I find myself automatically clocking where the exits are. I'm always watching to see if someone is standing too close to me. And instead of really paying attention to what people are saying, I'm just keeping one ear tuned to whatever noises are happening out in the hallway. I just can't seem to turn it off and be fully present anymore.
Overall, how much has this anxiety and fear been impacting your ability to work and your quality of life? Has it caused you significant problems in your day-to-day functioning?

Yeah, it definitely has. Um, my work has slipped enough that I’ve actually missed a few migration deadlines recently. And I've been completely avoiding key late deployments. It even came up in a performance review—I got called out for having conflicts with people, which... that just never used to happen before. 

And it's not just the daily work tasks. I've also pulled back from mentoring and the women-in-tech leadership events I used to be involved in. I just don’t feel steady or reliable enough to be there anymore. So, yeah, it's definitely causing some significant problems for me right now.
